doctrines.question: How much attention does the reality of angels and demons warrant, and does the biblical language name personal spiritual beings or the idiom of its age?
doctrines.framing: The existence of angels as created spiritual beings, and of Satan and demons as angels fallen through rebellion against God, is confessed across the Christian tradition, from the Fourth Lateran Council's definition of two orders of creatures to Westminster's treatment of providence over the fallen angels and the Thirty-Nine Articles' wider framework. What divides Christians is not whether such beings exist but how much attention the subject warrants in ordinary devotion, and whether the biblical language names real personal beings or is best read as the idiom of its own age.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places this at the second tier: what attention the subject warrants shapes devotional life without dividing on the gospel.

open.todo: Work out how much attention the subject of angels and demons warrants in ordinary devotion, and whether the demythologising reading has any merit or should be rejected outright.

positions.label: Real but undramatized
positions.hold: Angels and demons are real created spiritual beings, Satan and demons among them fallen through rebellion against God, resisted through ordinary prayer, Scripture, and the sacraments rather than through heightened attention or specialised practice.
positions.why: The historic confessions affirm a spiritual realm of angels and fallen angels but locate the Christian's resistance to evil within ordinary practice rather than a specialised discipline.
positions.vs: Treating angels and demons as a subject requiring specialised attention, heightened vigilance, or dedicated ministry beyond the ordinary means of grace.

held_by.citation: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 328-336; Fourth Lateran Council (1215), Canon 1
Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed (381), 'maker of heaven and earth, and of all things visible and invisible'

held_by.note: Not addressed in a dedicated article; affirmed within the Articles' wider trinitarian and creedal framework.
Affirmed through the ecumenical creeds the Book of Concord opens with rather than a dedicated article.

positions.label: Actively engaged
positions.hold: Angels and demons are real, and engaging demonic activity directly through prayer, spiritual warfare, and deliverance ministry is a normal and expected part of Christian life.
positions.why: Scripture depicts believers directly confronting demonic power in the name of Jesus, and pastoral experience of oppression calls for active engagement rather than mere affirmation of a doctrine.
positions.vs: Confining angelology and demonology to a settled doctrine confessed once and then set aside, rather than a live pastoral reality requiring active engagement.

held_by.citation: Assemblies of God, position paper, 'Ministry to Persons Oppressed by Demons' (1972)

held_by.note: Practice varies widely; common within charismatic-leaning independent congregations.
held_by.citation: Derek Prince, They Shall Expel Demons (1998)

sources.label: Assemblies of God position paper on demonic oppression

positions.label: Demythologized reading
positions.hold: The biblical language of angels, Satan, and demons is best read as the idiom of its ancient setting for impersonal forces of chaos, evil, and unbelief, not as reference to personal spiritual beings.
positions.why: Modern critical scholarship reads apocalyptic and mythic language as culturally conditioned expression of the age that produced it, rather than as literal claims about the existence of personal beings.
positions.vs: Treating the biblical language of angels and demons as reference to actual personal spiritual beings rather than as the idiom of its own age.
positions.orthodoxy_note: This reading is widely regarded by the historic traditions as abandoning what the creeds and Scripture affirm about a real spiritual realm, treating language they hold to name actual beings as ancient myth.
positions.learn_detail: This reading belongs mainly to modern critical biblical scholarship rather than to any tradition's confession; no registered tradition holds it as a confessional or majority position.

sources.label: Rudolf Bultmann's demythologising program as a point of reference

doctrines.learn_note: The existence of a spiritual realm inhabited by angels and fallen angels is not itself the contested question; the disagreement runs between how much devotional or pastoral attention it warrants and, at the margins, whether the biblical language names real beings at all.

doctrines.question: Do Psalm 82 and Deuteronomy 32:8-9 describe a real council of spiritual beings under God, or human judges and rhetorical figures?
doctrines.framing: Psalm 82 pictures God standing in the midst of a council of 'gods' whom he judges, and Deuteronomy 32:8-9 speaks of the nations being allotted according to the number of the 'sons of God'. The disagreement is over whether these texts describe an actual council of created spiritual beings placed under God's authority, an ancient Near Eastern idiom scholars have recently recovered, or whether 'gods' names human judges and 'sons of God' is a rhetorical or textual matter without such a council in view. This is a question of biblical scholarship rather than of any tradition's binding confession, and most traditions have no published position on it.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places this at the third tier: a live question in biblical scholarship that does not touch the gospel or govern practice.

open.todo: Work out whether Psalm 82's 'gods' and Deuteronomy 32:8-9's 'sons of God' describe a real council of created spiritual beings under God, or human judges and a rhetorical or textual figure without ontological reality.

positions.label: Real divine council
positions.hold: Psalm 82 and Deuteronomy 32:8-9 describe an actual council of created spiritual beings, the sons of God, whom God judges and to whom the nations were allotted, all subordinate to the God of Israel.
positions.why: Both texts read most naturally in their ancient Near Eastern setting as describing real spiritual beings under God's rule, a reading recovered by recent scholarship on Israel's cultural context.
positions.vs: Reading the same council language as a description of human judges or as a rhetorical figure without any real spiritual beings in view.
positions.learn_detail: This reading is most associated with the biblical scholarship of Michael Heiser and the wider study of Israel's ancient Near Eastern context; it is a scholarly position rather than a confessional one, and no registered tradition has adopted it formally.

positions.label: Human judges reading
positions.hold: The 'gods' of Psalm 82 are human judges or rulers whom God indicts for injustice, and Deuteronomy 32:8-9's 'sons of God' is best read without positing a literal council of spiritual beings governing the nations.
positions.why: Jesus himself applies Psalm 82's 'gods' to those to whom the word of God came, reading the term as a title for human officeholders rather than as reference to spiritual beings.
positions.vs: Reading the 'gods' judged in the council and the 'sons of God' allotted the nations as real created spiritual beings rather than as human officeholders or a rhetorical figure.

held_by.citation: John Calvin, Commentary on the Psalms (1557), on Psalm 82

doctrines.learn_note: This is a live question in Old Testament scholarship, not a confessional dividing line; most traditions have simply never addressed it, and an empty held_by list here reflects that rather than an oversight.

doctrines.question: Who are the 'sons of God' who take human wives in Genesis 6:1-4, and what does the passage describe?
doctrines.framing: Genesis 6:1-4 reports 'sons of God' taking the daughters of men as wives, producing the Nephilim, immediately before God's judgment in the flood. The oldest attested reading identifies the sons of God as angelic beings, the Watchers, who transgressed their created order; this reading stands behind 1 Enoch and is cited as history by 2 Peter and Jude and by most of the ante-Nicene Fathers. Later interpreters proposed that the sons of God are the godly line of Seth intermarrying with Cain's line, or that they are ancient kings and rulers claiming divine status. This is a question of biblical interpretation on which most confessions are silent.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places this at the third tier: an interpretive question about a single obscure passage that does not touch the gospel or govern practice.

open.todo: Work out whether Genesis 6's sons of God are angelic Watchers, the godly line of Seth, or ancient kings, and whether the ancient Enochic reading should be given weight simply because it is oldest.

positions.label: Sethite line
positions.hold: The sons of God in Genesis 6 are the godly line of Seth, whose intermarriage with the ungodly line of Cain corrupted the covenant line and provoked the judgment of the flood.
positions.why: Genesis has just traced the line of Seth as those who 'call upon the name of the Lord', and 'sons of God' elsewhere in the Old Testament can denote Israel or the covenant people rather than angelic beings.
positions.vs: Reading the sons of God as angelic beings who transgressed the created order rather than as the covenant line of Seth intermarrying with the ungodly line of Cain.

held_by.citation: John Calvin, Commentary on Genesis (1554), on Genesis 6:2
Keil and Delitzsch, Commentary on the Old Testament, on Genesis 6

positions.label: Angelic Watchers
positions.hold: The sons of God in Genesis 6 are angelic beings, Watchers, who abandoned their created order to take human wives, a transgression of cosmic boundaries that provoked the flood.
positions.why: This is the reading attested in 1 Enoch and cited as history by 2 Peter and Jude, and it was the dominant reading of most ante-Nicene Fathers before later interpreters proposed the Sethite alternative.
positions.vs: Treating the sons of God as merely the human line of Seth, when the term 'sons of God' elsewhere in the Old Testament names heavenly beings and the oldest interpreters read the passage as angelic transgression.
positions.orthodoxy_note: This is the oldest attested reading, held by most ante-Nicene Fathers and cited by two New Testament epistles, but it is disputed by later and modern interpreters who regard an angel-human union as theologically or exegetically untenable; no ecumenical council has settled the question.
positions.learn_detail: This reading is not a modern novelty: it stands behind 1 Enoch, is treated as history in 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 1:6, and was held by Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, and Tertullian among others, before Augustine's preference for the Sethite reading became dominant in the West.

positions.label: Divine kings
positions.hold: The sons of God in Genesis 6 are ancient kings or dynastic rulers who claimed divine sonship and exercised despotic power, including the taking of multiple wives, provoking God's judgment on human tyranny.
positions.why: Ancient Near Eastern royal ideology regularly styled kings as sons of the gods, and the passage's concern with the seizing of wives fits a critique of royal excess better than either the Sethite or angelic reading.
positions.vs: Reading the sons of God as either the covenant line of Seth or as angelic beings, rather than as human rulers claiming divine status.

held_by.note: A minority reading among Reformed scholars, distinct from the tradition's more common Sethite reading.
held_by.citation: Meredith G. Kline, 'Divine Kingship and Genesis 6:1-4', Westminster Theological Journal 24 (1962)

sources.label: Divine Kingship and Genesis 6:1-4
sources.citation: Meredith G. Kline, Westminster Theological Journal 24 (1962)

doctrines.learn_note: The angelic reading is the oldest attested, not a modern novelty invented by recent scholarship; the Sethite reading became dominant later, chiefly through Augustine's influence, and the divine-king reading is a modern minority proposal within the wider conversation.

reformed.hold: Most Reformed interpreters read the sons of God as the godly line of Seth; a minority within the tradition reads them instead as ancient kings claiming divine status.
reformed.note: Kline's divine-kingship reading is a real minority stream within Reformed scholarship, not the tradition's common view.
reformed.citation: John Calvin, Commentary on Genesis (1554), contrasted with Meredith G. Kline, Westminster Theological Journal 24 (1962)
